pieces.title: A Tale of Five Mangoes
pieces.body:
He shouldn’t be here
                                                  He is a good Christian boy
                                                           His friends laugh
“It’s no devil's ploy”
                                                So he looks at the mangoes
                                                    The forbidden fruits
                                                           Up Kojo goes
                                                    With his loyal druids
                                               He steadies his wheelchair
                                                    Their getaway vehicle
                                        There's a giggle from up the tree
                                                   Why are they so free?
                                      “Hurry!”
                                             He whisper-shouts
                                                     Mangoes come raining down
                                             Little Kwame wears a frown
                                      But does his best to catch them all
                                               They should be more careful
                                                                 Lest they              fall
                                                      He has five now
                                             And still wears the frown
                                                Many surround him
                                   They'll get them when they return
                                 There's a stir inside and everyone's still
                Who else could they expect but the one who pays the bill?
                                                         The creaking door sends everyone running
Left on the floor is our poor little Kwame

pieces.title: The Thing that came Home
pieces.body:
The leaves whispered their dirges
I did not answer.
The wind passed, carrying the scent of my father’s house
but I did not know the road.
My head burned with the fire of distant drums,
my bones remembered what my heart had buried.
The bell rings in the shrine of my skull.
I beat the air with trembling hands,
and silence, like a priest,
blessed me         for a moment.
But the bell tolls again.
It tolls for me.
I staggered into the house of my name,
washed my face in the bowl of forgetting.
The walls murmured stories I could not remember.
The children wept in the corner of the room
faces of mourning
but I could not wear their sorrow.
Were they mine?
Were they from the womb I had once touched with laughter?
And there, at the foot of the hearth,
she lay.
Still.
Not sleeping.
I called her name.
The name did not return.
I called again.
But the gods had already written her silence
on the back of my soul.
So I stood
alone
beside the thing that came home.
It was me.
And it was her.

pieces.title: My Suicide Note
pieces.body:
Again I feel worthless
My life and strife a balance between absence and nonsense
I laugh sadly as I recount my mistakes
Unable to retrace the path to my past and I
Think about all the things I could and should have done right
The worthless nature of a broken-down kiosk I now call home
The sun hitting me hard in a dreamless sleep
And now I’m awake and still living my nightmare
I stop and take a while to stare
Into the emptiness of the emptiness I created
And my doubt grows stronger
I can no longer accept this blessed curse of life
And so wind, when you carry my note into the sky
Please hear my cry and send this to a dying soul to learn from my mistakes
For if my life was nothing but Gehenna
My death might lead someone to paradise
I kick the stool from beneath my feet
And hang lifelessly
Finally succumbing to defeat

pieces.title: The borrowed Suit
pieces.subtitle: An opening
pieces.body:
Kweku owned exactly one good suit, and it belonged to his cousin. He had borrowed it for a funeral three years ago and the funeral, in a sense, had never quite ended. There was always another one to attend, another reason the suit could not yet go home.
His cousin had stopped asking. This, Kweku decided, was a form of generosity, and he intended to honour it for as long as the lining held.
The suit, for its part, had developed a reputation that exceeded Kweku entirely. Over three years it had attended more funerals than most pastors and had acquired, by sheer attendance, a perfumed authority. When Kweku arrived at a gathering, strangers shifted along the bench to make room. The suit implied he was someone. A grieving nephew. A man from the bank. Somebody whose presence settled accounts.
He had refined the thing into a discipline. He knew which families distributed cloth and which merely distributed grief, which canopies offered shade and which offered surveillance, which funerals served the good schnapps and which quietly watered it after the third bottle. Other men went to funerals to mourn. Kweku went to maintain a portfolio.
There were costs, naturally. The suit required upkeep the way a marriage requires patience. He had an arrangement with Auntie Mansa at the dry cleaner's, who by now knew the suit far more intimately than she knew him, and who had once, while pressing a sleeve, asked after his health as though addressing the jacket directly. The lining had begun to whisper its complaints. He honoured them. A promise was a promise, even one nobody had made.
Then came the Saturday he had not planned to work.
The invitation arrived properly this time, by way of a cousin of a cousin, a thing of stiff card and gold lettering, and it requested his presence with a warmth that he found, on reflection, suspicious. He went, of course. He always went. He arrived in the suit, took his customary seat near the front where the bereaved could see that the family was well represented, and only then lifted his eyes to the great photograph hung above the casket.
It was his cousin.
He sat very still while the brass band laboured through a hymn. He understood, dimly, that he was now attending the one funeral the suit had been travelling towards all along, and that the lining had known before he did.
It was the widow who said it, leaning across to him with the particular gentleness reserved for delicate negotiations. They had searched the house, she explained, and could not find anything fine enough to bury him in. The man had owned exactly one good suit, and it had gone missing years ago. But here, she said, touching his sleeve the way Auntie Mansa touched it, was something almost exactly right.
So Kweku lowered his cousin into the ground in the one good suit, and walked home in a borrowed length of mourning cloth, lighter than he had been in three years, and emptier in a way he could not name.
The following Saturday, at the funeral of a man he had never met, he found himself admiring, with professional interest, the cut of a stranger's blazer.

pieces.title: The Day He Chose (1)
pieces.body:
He had told her yes on a Tuesday, which was already a kind of lie. Not the yes itself, but the Tuesday, the ordinariness of it, as though yes were a thing that could be said on a Tuesday the way one says pass the salt or the rain is coming. Ama had looked at him across the table with eyes that had been waiting so long they had learned to look like they were not waiting, and he had said yes, and she had smiled the smile of a woman who has stopped believing in smiles and is therefore undone by one.
That had been fourteen months ago.
The wedding had been planned for April, then June, then the following January. He had moved each date with the gentleness of a man who believes he is being kind, offering reasons that were true enough to be believed and false enough to be reasons. Work. His mother's health. The hall that was double-booked. Ama had listened to each one with the patience of a woman who has decided that patience is the only weapon left to her, and she had said of course, of course, and somewhere behind her eyes a small thing was dying so slowly neither of them could hear it.
He was not a bad man. This was the cruelest thing about him. He loved Ama the way men love things they are afraid of losing and more afraid of keeping. He thought about her in the mornings with a tenderness that surprised him, and at night sometimes, lying beside her, he felt the warmth of her breathing and it seemed to him the best thing in the world, this warmth, and he could not understand why he kept scheduling it away.
His friends said he had cold feet. He accepted this explanation because it was available. But it was not cold feet. It was something older and less forgivable, a belief buried too deep in him to excavate, that joy was a thing that happened to other people, that happiness, once grasped, would dissolve in his hands like the cheap dye on a new cloth in the first rain. He had seen too many things dissolve. He had learned to keep his hands at his sides.
The final date was set for a Saturday in October, and this time he did not move it. He was not sure why. Perhaps Ama's silence had changed its quality and become less like waiting and more like conclusion. Perhaps he had simply grown tired of the weight of his own hesitation, which had grown heavier each month until it was the heaviest thing in his life, heavier than the marriage he was avoiding. He told his mother. He told his friends. He bought a suit, a good one, and hung it on the back of the door where he could see it each morning, a pale grey flag of his own surrender.
On the morning of the wedding he woke early. The light came through the curtains thin and golden, the kind of light that belongs to important days. He lay still for a moment, feeling the quality of the silence, and found to his surprise that he was not afraid. He was something else, something that had no name yet, something that sat in his chest like a door standing open onto a room he had never entered.
He dressed slowly. The suit fit well. He looked at himself in the mirror for a long time, the way a man looks when he is trying to recognize himself, and what he saw was not a man afraid but a man arriving, late and breathless, at something he should have run toward years ago.
He called Ama. She answered on the first ring.
"I'm coming," he said.
"I know," she said. Her voice was full of a morning he had not yet earned and she was giving it to him anyway, freely, the way she had always given things. Too freely, too fully, with both hands open.
He got in the car at half past nine. The roads were quiet, the city not yet loud with itself. He drove with the windows down, the October air moving through the car, touching his face. He was thinking about her hands. He was thinking about the table on that Tuesday, the ordinariness of the yes, how he wished now he had said it on a better day, a day with light like this, a day when the air moved like this, so she would have known from the weather alone that he meant it.
He was thinking this when the truck came from the junction on his left, not slowing, its driver perhaps blinded by the low October sun, perhaps asleep, perhaps simply one of those agents of the world's indifference that move among us unseen until the moment they are not. There was no time to think. There was barely time to be.
The sound was enormous and then there was no sound at all.

pieces.title: What We Mean by Postcolonial
pieces.subtitle: a word, unpacked
pieces.body:
The word arrives heavy with seminars, but the idea underneath it is plain enough to share at a table. It asks a simple question. After the soldiers and the flags have gone, who still owns the story? Whose language do we dream in, whose history fills the schoolbook, whose name is on the building?

Scholarship dresses this question in long clothes. Our task, when we write for a wider room, is to let it walk in barefoot and still be taken seriously. Empire leaves furniture behind. The soldiers sail home, but the language stays, and so do the borders drawn by strangers, the economy still wired to send its best goods outward, the history lesson that begins on the day the ships arrived, as though the centuries before were an empty room. Postcolonialism is the habit of noticing the furniture and asking who arranged it this way, and whether it has to stay.

Some of that furniture sits inside the head. This was Frantz Fanon's hard insight: a long enough rule does not merely govern a people, it teaches them to look at themselves through the ruler's eyes, to find their own faces a little wanting. Edward Said showed the trick from the other side, how the powerful build an image of the distant and the conquered, then call that image knowledge. And Ngugi wa Thiong'o pressed the question of language until it ached. If you dream, argue and pray in the tongue that was handed to you by force, in what sense is the dream your own?

It would be tidy to answer all this by going back, by scrubbing off every borrowed thing and returning to some clean original self. But there is no clean original self left, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of fantasy. The cultures that came through colonisation are mixed now, layered, fluent in more than one inheritance. The honest task is not erasure but choice: to hold up each inherited thing, the language, the faith, the legal code, the table manners, and decide freely which to keep, which to refuse, and which to remake into something that finally answers to us.

Which returns us to the question at the table. After the flags come down, the last territory still under dispute is the story itself. Postcolonialism, stripped of its long clothes, is simply the long work of taking back the pen.

pieces.title: On Laughing in the Lecture Hall
pieces.subtitle: why comedy belongs in serious work
pieces.body:
We are taught to mistrust laughter in serious rooms, as though a joke were a leak in the argument. Yet the oldest teachers in this part of the world knew better. The storyteller by the fire did not choose between instruction and delight. She smuggled the lesson inside the laugh, and the laugh carried it further than solemnity ever could.

A classroom that never laughs is not more rigorous. It is only quieter about what it has failed to make memorable. Consider what a joke actually demands of the mind. To land it, you have to hold two ideas at once, the expected and the swerve, and feel the gap between them. That is not a softer form of thinking. It is the same move as analysis: the noticing that things could be otherwise, that the obvious arrangement is only one arrangement. A student who laughs at the right moment has understood something. The laugh is the receipt.

Comedy is also where a people keep their most dangerous truths. When power cannot be named plainly, it gets named sideways, in the proverb that bites, the song that mocks the chief, the figure who plays the fool so he can say what no serious man is allowed to say. The court jester survived precisely because he was funny; the funniness was a passport that let hard truths cross a guarded border. To teach satire, then, is not to teach a lesser art. It is to hand students one of the oldest tools their culture built for speaking to power and surviving the conversation.

There is a worry worth taking seriously, that laughter cheapens, that it lets everyone off the hook before the difficult thing has been felt. Sometimes it does. A joke can be an exit as easily as a door. But the answer is not to ban laughter from the room; it is to teach the difference between the laugh that closes a question and the laugh that opens one. The first lets you walk away comfortable. The second leaves a splinter under the comfort, the small unease that sends you back to the matter when the room has emptied.

So let the lecture hall laugh. Not because the work is unserious, but because seriousness was never the same thing as solemnity. The fireside teacher knew this before we built the halls. The lesson smuggled inside delight is the one still lodged in the body the next morning, when the solemn ones have all been forgotten.

pieces.title: When the Wounded Begin to Wound
pieces.subtitle: A South Africa gone south
pieces.body:
A wound that is bandaged before it is cleaned does not heal. It festers quietly under the dressing, and one day it breaks open in places nobody expected.
That is what I think of when I watch the news from South Africa.
Crowds are marching through Johannesburg, Durban and Pretoria, led most visibly by Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and her March and March movement, telling fellow Black Africans to pack up and go home. Shops looted. People beaten. Ghanaians airlifted back to Accra. And here is the bitter irony: the targets of this rage are almost never the people who actually built the system that impoverished Black South Africans. They are Nigerians, Zimbabweans, Ghanaians, Malawians. The neighbours. The cousins.
Psychologists have a name for this. Intergenerational trauma. The idea, supported by decades of research from Holocaust survivor studies to post-apartheid scholarship, is that unprocessed pain does not die with the generation that suffered it. It is transmitted. Through parenting, through silence, through poverty, through the stories families tell and the ones they cannot bring themselves to tell. Frantz Fanon saw it even earlier: the colonised, unable to strike upward at the coloniser, learns to strike sideways at his own reflection.
South Africa only dismantled apartheid in 1994. That is barely one generation ago. Many of the people marching today were raised by parents who were legally classified as less than human in their own country. And yet, three decades later, the economic architecture of apartheid still stands largely intact. Whiteness still signals wealth, authority and arrival. The anger that should interrogate that structure finds a softer target instead: the Somali shopkeeper, the Ghanaian trader, the Zimbabwean nurse.
This is what happens when a nation is told to celebrate reconciliation before it has been allowed to grieve. Truth commissions gave us testimony, yes. But testimony without repair is a wound described, not a wound treated.
So when we in Ghana, in Nigeria, in Zimbabwe respond with our own anger, and the anger is legitimate, we should also respond with clarity. What we are watching is not simply hatred. It is haunting. It is what pain does when it is papered over for thirty years and told to smile for the cameras of the rainbow nation.
Healing cannot be decreed. It has to be done. Land, wages, schools, dignity, memory. Until then, the scars will keep speaking, and they will keep speaking in the wrong direction.
May South Africa find the courage to turn its grief toward its true source. And may the rest of us never forget that a traumatised people can become dangerous, not because they are wicked, but because nobody ever helped them put the pain down.

pieces.title: Born to the Craft
pieces.subtitle: West Africa's Hereditary Artists
pieces.body:
Imagine being born already knowing what you would become. Not because your parents pushed you, and not because you showed a talent for it, but because your family had always done this one thing, and so would you, and so would your children. You would be a blacksmith, or a musician, or a worker in leather. You would almost certainly marry someone from a family that did the same. This was the reality for millions of people across West Africa, and in many places it still shapes who marries whom.

The historian Tal Tamari spent years tracing how this came to be. Her work covers more than fifteen peoples spread across at least fourteen modern states, from Mali and Senegal to the edges of Ghana, Liberia and the Algerian Sahara. The pattern she found is remarkably consistent, and once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE

In most of these societies, everyone belonged to one of three groups. At the top were the freeborn, usually farmers or, among the Fulani, herders. At the bottom were the enslaved. In between sat a third group, set apart not by wealth but by trade: the families who made and the families who remembered.

The makers were the smiths, the woodcarvers, the leatherworkers, the potters and the weavers. The rememberers were the bards, known to many today by the French word griot. These were not casual occupations. A freeborn man could not simply pick up a hammer and start forging iron, or sing in public, or work leather. Those activities belonged to specific families, passed down like an inheritance.

Here is the detail that surprises most people. Although these artisan families ranked below the freeborn, they could never be enslaved. A noble captured in war might lose everything and end up in chains. A blacksmith never could. So the people who looked lower on the ladder held a kind of protection the so-called higher people lacked.

THE KEEPERS OF MEMORY

Of all these groups, the bards are the easiest to fall in love with. They were the living libraries of their societies. They held the genealogies, sang the praises of kings, settled disputes between families and carried messages between the powerful. When the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited the Mali empire in the 1350s, he noticed something that tells you everything about their status: the king did not speak to his people directly. He spoke through an interpreter, and that interpreter was also the finest musician at court.

The respect could curdle into something stranger. Among the Wolof and Serer, bards were not buried in the ground at all. Their bodies were placed inside the hollow trunks of baobab trees, because people feared that burying a bard would bring drought. When Portuguese sailors first described these musicians in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, they were so puzzled by the social separation that they decided the bards must be Jews. The mistake stuck so firmly that in Portuguese Creole, the word for bard is still judeus.

WHERE DID IT ALL BEGIN

The most thrilling part of Tamari's work is the detective method. How do you date something that left almost no written records? She used everything available: the accounts of Arab travellers, the great chronicles of Timbuktu, the journals of European sailors, oral epics, and, cleverly, language itself.

Words travel when institutions travel. Tamari gathered sixty-seven different terms for these artisan groups across eleven languages and found that most of them were borrowed. The words for bard, in particular, were passed from one people to the next like a loan, which tells you the institution itself was being passed along. The words for blacksmith, by contrast, were mostly homegrown. People knew how to work iron long before they organised smiths into a separate hereditary group.

Following these clues, she reached a striking conclusion. The caste systems now found among more than fifteen peoples did not spring up independently all over the region. They radiated outward from at most three original centres: the Manding, the Soninke and the Wolof. Migration did the rest.

As for the beginning of the beginning, Tamari points to the famous Sunjata epic, the founding story of the Mali empire. In it, the villain is Sumanguru Kante, a sorcerer king whose power comes from iron and from a magical xylophone he guards jealously. When Sunjata's bard learns to play that instrument, the scene reads like a transfer of mystical power from the old order to the new. Tamari reads the epic's contradictions as a memory of the moment, sometime in the thirteenth century, when smiths and singers were quietly stripped of political power and reshaped into the groups we recognise today.

NOT FROZEN IN TIME
It would be easy to picture all this as something rigid and ancient, sealed in place forever. It was never that. Families changed trades. A group of woodcarvers might give up wood for music and dance. Bards drifted up in rank, leatherworkers drifted down, and newcomers were quietly absorbed into local groups until their foreign origins vanished from memory. The system bent and reshaped itself in every generation, which is exactly why it survived.

What lingers, in the end, is the griot. A person born to carry the memory of a whole people, to keep the names and the deeds alive, to speak so that a king need not. In a world without writing, that was not a low calling at all. It was one of the most powerful jobs a society could invent.
